courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Training: the loss, clone, split, prune and opacity reset
question: During training a thin railing is rendered as one long, blurry Gaussian with a large positional gradient. Its largest scale is 5 percent of the scene extent. What does the default density control do?
options: Clone it, because large gradients always mean missing geometry
Prune it, because its gradient is large
Reset its opacity to zero right away
Split it into two Gaussians with scales divided by 1.6
explain: The gradient passes the 0.0002 threshold, and the Gaussian is larger than 1 percent of the scene extent, so it counts as over-reconstruction: split. Cloning is for small Gaussians; pruning depends on opacity and size, not gradient.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: LL/SC: watching the location instead of its value
question: Why can't a portable lock-free stack on RISC-V simply rely on LR/SC to avoid ABA in pop?
options: RISC-V has no LR/SC instructions on RV64
Pop must load t->next between LR and SC, which falls outside a constrained loop, so eventual success is not guaranteed
SC never fails, so it behaves exactly like CAS
explain: Constrained LR/SC loops forbid loads between LR and SC. The pop's dependent load makes the loop unconstrained, and the spec says such sequences might never succeed on some implementations, so portable code needs a fallback.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Interaction effects and Shapley values
question: Stages A and B both fix the same failure, so they are almost fully redundant. Each adds +0.04 alone, and together they add +0.045. What do leave-one-out deltas show?
options: Both look nearly useless (about +0.005 each), even though removing both costs 0.045
Both look worth +0.04 each
A looks worth +0.045 and B worth 0
Leave-one-out cannot be computed for redundant stages
explain: Removing either one leaves the other to cover the failure, so each loses only 0.045 - 0.04 = 0.005. Leave-one-out undercounts redundant stages; Shapley gives each +0.0225 here. This is Q and H in the toy.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
question: A support-bot team can run one attempt per customer and has no way to verify success before the customer sees it. Which metric should drive their model choice?
options: pass@8, because more attempts give a better estimate
pass^1 alone, because only one attempt is made
pass^k for k > 1, because it rewards succeeding every time across conversation variations
pass@1 on a coding benchmark
explain: Each customer is a fresh trial of a similar task. pass^k measures whether the agent succeeds consistently across k such variations, which is the reliability the team needs. pass@k assumes you can retry and pick a winner, which they cannot.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
question: Which item is safest to drop first when the context is filling up?
options: The system prompt's safety rules
The user's original task statement
The most recent tool result
The raw output of a test run from 20 steps ago that the agent already acted on
explain: An old tool result that has already been consumed is the classic low-value token: the agent's later actions reflect it. That is why tool result clearing is the lightest-touch compaction. The task, rules and most recent observations are what the next step depends on.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Main context vs external context: paging memory like an OS
question: In MemGPT, a message was evicted from the FIFO queue during a flush. Which statement is true?
options: The message is gone; only the recursive summary remains
It is still in the prompt, but compressed
It was moved into working context automatically
It is out of the prompt but still stored in recall storage, reachable through a search function call
explain: The queue manager writes every message to recall storage when it arrives. Eviction removes it from main context and folds it into the recursive summary, but the original stays in recall storage, which the LLM can search with a function call. Working context only changes when the LLM itself calls a write function.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
question: Your memory system scores well on recall but often answers with an old address after users move. Which LongMemEval ability is failing, and where would you fix it first?
options: Abstention; add a confidence threshold to the reader
Information extraction; use a bigger embedding model
Knowledge updates; fix the write path so a new address updates or invalidates the old one, and keep timestamps
Multi-session reasoning; retrieve more memories per query
explain: Recognizing that the user's information changed is LongMemEval's knowledge-update ability. Recall is fine, so a better retriever or more results would only surface both addresses. The fix is on the write path (UPDATE, DELETE or invalidation) plus timestamps so the reader can tell which is current.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: When more samples hurt, and how agreement helps
question: In CodeT, group A has 2 solutions that pass the same 5 tests and group B has 6 solutions that pass the same 2 tests. Which group does dual execution agreement prefer?
options: B, because its score 6 x 2 = 12 exceeds 2 x 5 = 10
A, because its solutions pass more tests
Neither; CodeT breaks ties at random
A, because CodeT only counts tests passed
explain: The score is |Sx| times |Sy|: 12 for B and 10 for A. Agreement among many solutions counts as much as test count, which is how CodeT resists a few wrong tests.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Where tasks come from: SWE-Gym, R2E-Gym, SWE-RL and hubs
question: SWE-Gym's headline training gains came from which procedure?
options: Fine-tuning on successful trajectories sampled in the environment (rejection sampling fine-tuning)
Multi-turn GRPO with a similarity reward
PPO with a learned value model over test outcomes
Pretraining on 6 TB of Docker images
explain: The paper uses rejection sampling fine-tuning, also called filtered behavior cloning, as its policy improvement method. An environment with a reliable reward supports that as well as RL.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
question: Why does MatterGen diffuse fractional coordinates with a wrapped Normal instead of an ordinary Gaussian?
options: Because wrapped Normals are cheaper to sample
Because fractional coordinates are periodic: x = 0.98 and x = 0.02 are close, and the noise must reach the uniform distribution on the cell
Because the lattice is always cubic during generation
Because atom types are discrete
explain: An ordinary Gaussian ignores that the cell wraps around: it pushes atoms outside [0, 1) and treats 0.98 and 0.02 as far apart. Wrapping folds probability mass back in, matches the minimum-image geometry from lesson 1, and gives a clean 'anywhere in the cell' noise limit.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks, limits, and content credentials for images
question: A provider uses a green list seeded by the previous 5 tokens (h = 5, gamma = 0.5). An attacker edits 1 token in the middle of a long text. Roughly how many extra red tokens does that one edit create, in expectation?
explain: The edited token changes the seed for the next 5 positions, and each of those tokens is then green only by chance (probability 0.5), so about 2.5 extra red tokens. That is what the paper calls attack amplification, and why a small h or the self-hash scheme is suggested.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Replaying workloads to compare allocators
question: Why does trace_run write every byte of each block it allocates?
options: To make the pages resident, so VmRSS reflects the blocks as it would for a program that uses its memory
To slow the replay down to match the original program's speed
To zero memory, emulating calloc
To compute a checksum for trace inversion detection
explain: Untouched pages are often never backed by RAM, so an allocator that mmaps lazily would look unrealistically cheap. Writing the block (with 0x11 bytes) makes the RSS measurement meaningful. It is not zeroing and does not model the original timing.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
question: A system uses no-steal and no-force. After a crash, which work can recovery skip entirely?
options: Redo of committed transactions, because their pages were written at commit
Undo of uncommitted transactions, because their changes never reached the data pages
Both, because the log already contains everything
Neither, because the log may be incomplete
explain: No-steal guarantees no uncommitted change was ever written to a data page, so there is nothing to undo. No-force means committed changes may still be missing on disk, so redo is still required.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
question: One page, all records for it. Before the crash: updates 1 and 2, the page is written to disk, updates 3 and 4, a partial rollback writes CLRs 4' and 3', then updates 5 and 6. The transaction is a loser. What does ARIES do at restart?
options: Redo nothing, since the transaction is a loser; undo 6, 5, 2, 1
Redo 1 through 6; undo 6, 5, 4', 3'
explain: This is Fig. 13 of the ARIES paper. Redo repeats everything after the page write, CLRs included. Undo follows PrevLSN from 6 to 5, then reaches CLR 3', whose UndoNextLSN points at 2, so 4 and 3 are not undone again. Then 2 and 1.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
question: You want to cluster 50,000 support tickets by topic with an API that offers search_query, search_document, classification and clustering types. Which setup matches the docs?
options: search_query for half the tickets and search_document for the other half
The clustering type for every ticket
search_document for all tickets, since they are stored documents
No input type, because clustering does not use cosine
explain: Clustering compares tickets with each other, a symmetric task, so every text gets the same role. Cohere documents a clustering type for exactly this, and Nomic uses a clustering prefix on both sides. Splitting the tickets across query and document types would make the halves systematically different.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
question: A 429 arrives with `Retry-After: 30`. Your backoff ceiling for this attempt would be 0.8 s. What should the client do?
options: Sleep a random time in [0, 0.8] s, since full jitter is best
Sleep 0.8 s, then 30 s if the next attempt fails
Wait at least 30 s, with a little added randomness, before retrying
Ignore the header; it is only used with 503
explain: Retry-After is the server telling you when capacity will be back. RFC 6585 allows it on 429, Anthropic says to wait that many seconds, and OpenAI treats it as a minimum and suggests adding a small random delay. Retrying after 0.8 s just produces another 429 and spends request budget.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
question: What makes Rust's `async fn` a *stackless* coroutine?
options: It cannot call other functions
It runs on the caller's stack forever and never suspends
It suspends by returning to its caller, and the data needed to resume lives in a separate object
It is only allowed inside a runtime with one thread
explain: Stackless means no private stack: suspending is a return, and the locals that must survive the suspension are stored in a separate state object (the future). Stackful coroutines instead keep a whole stack per coroutine.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
question: Two threads each run a plain (non-atomic) `counter++` once on a shared counter that starts at 0. Which statement is right?
options: The result is always 2, because each increment is one machine instruction on x86
The result is 1 or 2, and in C or C++ the program has undefined behavior
The result is always 1, because both threads read 0
It is safe as long as the counter is declared volatile
explain: Depending on the schedule, both reads can happen before either write (result 1) or not (result 2). Being one x86 instruction does not help: the core still loads and stores separately. And since the accesses conflict without synchronization, the C++ standard calls this a data race, which is undefined behavior. volatile does not make it atomic.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
question: Using the same padding rule, how many YAMNet patches (score rows) does a 10.0 s clip produce?
options: 10, one per second
21, because the last partial hop adds an extra patch
explain: The 10 s clip is padded to 161,520 samples, giving 1008 STFT frames and $1 + \lfloor (1008 - 96)/48 \rfloor = 20$ patches. Twenty patches at a 0.48 s hop span 0 to 10.08 s.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: AST and SpecAugment: patches, attention and masked bands
question: A teammate implements frequency masking by writing -80 (very quiet in their dB scale) into masked bins of unnormalized log-mel features. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, silence is the most natural mask value
Masks must be applied to the waveform, not the spectrogram
Frequency masks must always cover exactly F bins
The masked block becomes an extreme, easy-to-spot value instead of the mean; SpecAugment normalizes to zero mean so 0 equals the mean
explain: In the paper, features are normalized to zero mean and masked values are set to 0, which is the mean. Filling with an extreme value creates an unnatural pattern the model can learn to detect, and it shifts the input statistics compared with test time.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Tracking sources and checking every citation
question: A report has 20 cited claims. Every URL returns HTTP 200, and an entailment judge finds 15 of the cited passages support their claims. What is the citation precision, and what does the 200 check add?
options: 1.00; the 200 check proves the citations are correct
0.75; the 200 check is redundant once you run the judge
0.25; five failures out of twenty
0.75; the 200 check only rules out invented sources, not unsupported claims
explain: Precision is 15 / 20 = 0.75. Resolving URLs rules out fabricated sources cheaply but says nothing about support. It is not redundant: the judge needs the fetched page to compare against, and a dead link is a separate failure to report.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero
question: A weight matrix has gamma = 0.4. Which ternary values do the weights [0.5, -0.1, -0.9, 0.19] get?
explain: Divide by gamma: [1.25, -0.25, -2.25, 0.475]. Round: [1, 0, -2, 0], then clip -2 to -1. Note 0.475 is just under the 0.5 threshold, so 0.19 is switched off even though it is not tiny.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
question: A branch goes N, N, T repeating forever. Which predictor gets it right after warm-up?
options: A 2-bit counter, because it is biased toward N
A 1-bit last-outcome predictor
None, period-3 patterns are unpredictable
A two-level predictor with 2 bits of the branch's own history
explain: Period 3 is at most n + 1 with n = 2, and the three 2-bit histories NN, NT, TN are all different, so each gets its own counter. The 2-bit counter only learns the N bias and misses every T (33 percent misses).

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: When branchless loses, and how to measure it
question: `perf stat` reports 0.4 percent branch misses for your program, yet a profiler shows one loop is slow. Could a branch still be the problem?
options: No, under 1 percent misses means branches are irrelevant
Yes, the overall rate averages over billions of easy branches and can hide one hot branch that misses often
No, perf stat counts every misprediction twice
Only if the program is multi-threaded
explain: The aggregate rate is a ratio over all branches. A single unpredictable branch in the hot loop can dominate time while barely moving the total. Profile where the misses happen (for example `perf record -e branch-misses`).

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
question: A database uses 10 bits per key Bloom filters and has 8 sorted runs. A lookup for a key that exists only in the last run is issued. About how many file reads does it take, assuming filters and indexes are cached?
explain: The true hit costs 1 read. The 7 other runs each pass a false positive with about 0.82% probability: 7 x 0.0082 = 0.057 extra reads. Total about 1.06. 8 is the no-filter case; 0.07 is the expected cost for a missing key.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: LRU-K: evict by the K-th most recent reference
question: At time 20 a pool holds P (references at 4, 15, 19), Q (references at 12, 17) and R (one reference at 18). Under LRU-2, which page is evicted?
options: P, because its oldest reference (time 4) is the oldest in the pool
Q, because b(Q,2) = 8 is larger than b(P,2) = 5
R, because it has only one reference, so b(R,2) is infinite
Q, because its last reference is the oldest
explain: b(P,2) = 20 minus 15 = 5 (second most recent is 15, not 4). b(Q,2) = 20 minus 12 = 8. R has one reference, so its distance is infinite and it goes first. Option 2 would be right if R were not in the pool.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes
question: Which weakness is shared by strided and space patching but fixed by a patcher driven by prediction difficulty?
options: Both need a fixed vocabulary
Neither can split a word into more than one patch
Neither lets you tune the average patch size
Neither decides boundaries from how hard the upcoming bytes are to predict
explain: Strided patching cuts every P bytes, and space patching cuts at spaces; neither looks at how predictable the text is. Strided patching does let you tune P (so the third option is wrong for it), and neither uses a vocabulary.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
question: The Android team kept most of its existing C and C++ code but wrote new code in memory safe languages. What happened to the memory safety share of its vulnerabilities between 2019 and 2024?
options: It stayed near 70%, because old code still dominates
It rose, because FFI glue introduced new bugs
It fell from 76% to 24%
It fell to 0%, because Rust code has no unsafe
explain: The September 2024 Google Security Blog post reports 76% in 2019 and 24% in 2024. Their explanation: most vulnerabilities live in new or recently changed code, and vulnerability density decays as code ages, so stopping the inflow of new unsafe code pays off quickly.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: FFI: calling C from Rust without losing track of ownership
question: A C library returns `char *` from `lib_get_name()` and documents that callers must release it with `lib_free_name()`. How should the Rust wrapper free it?
options: Call `lib_free_name` (for example from a `Drop` impl) after copying the bytes out
Wrap it with `CString::from_raw` and let Rust drop it
Call `libc::free`, since all C strings come from malloc
Leave it: Rust frees foreign memory automatically at scope end
explain: `CString::from_raw` is only for pointers produced by `CString::into_raw`; on foreign memory it risks allocator corruption. The library may not use malloc at all, so its own release function is the only correct one. Rust never frees memory it does not own.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Writes, sharing between cores, and measuring your machine
question: A write-back, write-allocate L1d holds a dirty line. A new line maps to the same set and the LRU victim is that dirty line. What must happen?
options: The dirty line is simply dropped, because memory already has the value
The dirty line's data is written back to the next level before its slot is reused
The new access bypasses the cache because the set is dirty
Every other core's cache is invalidated
explain: Write-back defers the memory update until eviction, so the dirty bit means the next level is stale. Evicting the line forces a write-back. Dropping it would lose the write; that is only allowed for clean lines. Invalidation concerns other cores' copies, which a dirty line by definition does not have.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: The local replacement model makes every edge linear
question: Which nonlinearities does the local replacement model freeze at their observed values?
options: Attention patterns and normalization denominators
Only the CLT feature thresholds
The softmax over the output vocabulary
Nothing; it relies on gradients only
explain: Attention patterns and normalization denominators are frozen, and MLPs are replaced by CLT features plus error terms. The features' own JumpReLUs remain, which is why each feature's preactivation is linear in earlier activations but its activation is not.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself
question: Your logs show document X at rank 1 with CTR 0.20 and document Y at rank 5 with CTR 0.08. Under our model with $\theta_k = 1/k$, which is more relevant?
options: X, because its CTR is 2.5 times higher
Y: its relevance is 0.08 / 0.2 = 0.40, double X's 0.20
They are equally relevant; CTR differences are noise
It cannot be decided without human labels
explain: Divide CTR by the examination probability of the slot: X is 0.20 / 1 = 0.20 and Y is 0.08 / 0.2 = 0.40. Y wins. This is exactly the correction the rest of the course builds.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Why CLIP learns from captions instead of fixed labels
question: Why does CLIP project both encoders into one shared space and L2-normalize the result?
options: So images can be decoded back into captions
So a single dot product directly measures image-text similarity on a fixed scale
So the text encoder can reuse the image encoder's weights
Because normalization is what makes the encoders train from scratch
explain: With both vectors in the same space and of unit length, their dot product is their cosine similarity, a number between -1 and 1 that is comparable across every pair. CLIP has no decoder, the two towers share no weights, and training from scratch is a separate choice.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Image search with CLIP, the modality gap, and where it fails
question: You index both product photos and product descriptions in one CLIP vector index and query it with a photo. What does the modality gap predict?
options: Results skew toward other photos, because image embeddings sit in a separate region from text embeddings
Results are evenly mixed, because the space is shared
Results skew toward descriptions, because text embeddings are closer to every image
The query fails, because image queries need the text encoder
explain: Liang et al. show image and text embeddings form separate regions (mean distance 0.82 on MS-COCO for CLIP). An image query is therefore closer to images in general than to text, so same-modality items crowd the top results even when a description matches better.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: DBSCAN: core points, border points and noise
question: Which of these can DBSCAN do that k-means cannot, on the same data?
options: Guarantee the globally optimal clustering for its objective
Run without computing any distances
Return a chain-shaped cluster and label a far-away point as belonging to no cluster
Produce exactly the number of clusters you ask for
explain: Density connectivity can follow an arbitrary shape and leaves points outside every cluster as noise (label -1). k-means clusters are convex Voronoi cells and every point is assigned. The number of clusters is an output of DBSCAN, not an input, and both methods are distance-based.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Parquet on disk: row groups, column chunks, pages and a footer
question: Why does Parquet put the file metadata at the end of the file instead of the start?
options: Readers must scan the data before they can parse the schema
So the writer can stream row groups out in a single pass and record their offsets and stats afterwards
Because Thrift requires trailing headers
To make appends to an existing file cheap
explain: The spec says metadata is written after the data to allow single-pass writing: chunk offsets and statistics are only known once the chunks are written. Readers simply read the last 8 bytes first.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: SIMD, compiled queries and where columnar engines hit limits
question: A table is written as Parquet with 1 GB row groups and no page index, written in random order. Queries filter on customer_id = X and read 3 of 50 columns. Which change most reduces bytes read?
options: Enable AVX-512 in the query engine
Increase the engine's vector size to 1M
Convert the files to Arrow IPC for storage
Sort or cluster by customer_id when writing (and write a page index) so min/max stats can skip most groups and pages
explain: Column projection already limits reads to 3 columns. The remaining waste is reading groups that cannot contain X; clustering makes min/max ranges narrow so pruning works. SIMD and vector size affect CPU, not bytes read.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
question: Which part of a ThinLTO build is serial?
options: Compiling each source file
The thin link that merges summaries and decides imports
Optimizing each module's backend
Writing the final object files
explain: Compiles and backends run in parallel. Only the thin link is serial, and it is fast because it reads compact summaries rather than whole function bodies.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Coordinates: grounding a click and scaling it to the real display
question: Clicks land in the right area but often miss very small targets. Scaling is verified correct. Which fix matches the docs' guidance?
options: Send the screenshot at a higher resolution than the image limit so the API keeps detail
Switch the aspect ratio of the screenshot to 1:1 so the model counts pixels more easily
Keep zoom enabled so the model can inspect the region at full resolution, and keep the aspect ratio when resizing
Retry each click three times at random offsets of a few pixels
explain: The docs attribute right-area misses to tiny targets, detail lost when downscaling a large source, or distorted aspect ratio, and suggest zoom, cropping or capturing at lower DPI, and preserving aspect ratio. Oversized images are rejected, not kept. Random retries can click the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
question: Your lock-free queue test passed 50,000 times on an x86 laptop. A teammate says it is now safe to ship to Arm servers. What is the strongest objection?
options: 50,000 runs is too few; 5 million runs would be enough
x86 hardware keeps more orderings than Arm, so a missing Release or Acquire may simply be invisible there and still break on Arm
The test should have been run in debug mode instead of release mode
Lock-free code cannot be tested at all, only proven
explain: Running more often only samples more schedules of the same hardware memory model. Weak-ordering bugs that x86's stronger hardware ordering hides have probability zero there, so no count of x86 runs covers them. A tool that models the language memory model, like loom, can explore those executions.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
question: A CI job runs your C++ service's integration tests under `-fsanitize=thread` and reports nothing for months. Which statement is justified?
options: The service is free of data races
TSan is misconfigured, since every large program has races
The service cannot deadlock
No data race occurred, unordered by happens-before, on the code paths and synchronization these tests exercised
explain: TSan is a dynamic detector: it is precise about what it saw but blind to paths that never ran and to races hidden by incidental synchronization in this run. Clean reports are evidence about the executed paths only.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
question: You need a one-step text-to-image model and have no budget for training a new diffusion model, but you do have a strong pretrained latent diffusion model with classifier-free guidance. Which approach fits best?
options: Latent consistency distillation (LCM) or adversarial diffusion distillation from that model
Consistency training from scratch on pixels
Progressive distillation from 8192 steps in pixel space
Plain L2 regression from noise to random images
explain: LCM and ADD both start from an existing latent diffusion teacher and target 1 to 4 steps; LCM distills the guided ODE directly (about 32 A100 hours for its 768x768 model). CT from scratch means training a new model; PD takes many halving stages; noise-to-random-image regression learns the mean.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix
question: A Dynamo-style store uses N=3, W=2, R=2 with last-write-wins timestamps and no read write-back. Which anomaly can still occur?
options: A read missing a write that completed long ago
Two reads in sequence, the second returning an older value than the first while a write is in flight
A read returning a value that was never written
Writes being lost because W is not equal to N
explain: With W + R > N, every completed write is seen by later quorum reads. But during a write that has reached only some replicas, one read can see it and a later read can miss it, exactly the R2 then R3 pattern. ABD's write-back closes that gap.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Virtual nodes: many tokens per server smooth out the load
question: You run 20 nodes with 1 token each and see one node at 3x average load. Which change reduces the spread of per-node load most directly?
options: Switch the key hash from MD5 to a faster hash
Give each node about 100 tokens (virtual nodes)
Add 5 more nodes with 1 token each
Replicate every key to 3 nodes
explain: Spread comes from uneven arc sizes. With T tokens per node the relative spread falls roughly like 1/sqrt(T), so 100 tokens cuts it to around 10%. A different hash function does not change the geometry, more single-token nodes stay just as uneven, and replication multiplies storage without evening out arcs.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
question: With gauss on distance, offset 5 km, scale 20 km, decay 0.5: what does a candidate 25 km away score, and what does one 4 km away score?
explain: At 25 km, d = 25 - 5 = 20 = scale, so the score equals decay, 0.5. At 4 km the candidate is inside the offset, d = 0, so the score is 1.0.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
question: X and Y have domain {1,2,3} and the only constraint is X < Y. What does AC-3 leave?
options: X {1,2,3}, Y {1,2,3}, because no value is fixed yet
X {1,2}, Y {1,2,3}, because only the arc (X,Y) is revised
explain: Revising (X,Y) deletes X=3 (no larger Y); revising (Y,X) deletes Y=1 (no smaller X). X=1 is supported by Y=2 or 3, and X=2 by Y=3, so nothing else goes. AC-3 keeps every value that appears in some solution of a single constraint; it does not pick a solution.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: A container is a process with a narrowed view
question: Which statement about a container and a virtual machine running on the same node is correct?
options: Both run their own kernel, so a kernel panic affects only one of them
The container has its own scheduler, so cgroup limits are advisory
The container's threads are scheduled by the host kernel, which also serves their page faults and TCP connections
A container cannot share a CPU with other work
explain: The container's threads are plain tasks on the host kernel's run queues. That is what makes containers start in milliseconds, and also what makes the node's kernel shared fate for everything on it. A virtual machine does run a second kernel, at the cost of booting one.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Probes, Services and DNS: liveness is not readiness
question: Every replica of a service uses one endpoint for both liveness and readiness, and that endpoint returns 503 while the database is unreachable. The database restarts for 90 seconds. What happens?
options: Only readiness is affected, so traffic pauses and then resumes
The Service keeps routing, because liveness does not touch EndpointSlices
The scheduler moves the pods to other nodes
Every replica fails liveness and is restarted together, so recovery is delayed by cold starts on top of the database outage
explain: A liveness failure restarts the container; a readiness failure only removes it from the EndpointSlices. Because one shared endpoint drives both, a dependency outage triggers both everywhere at once: the fleet goes NotReady and is also restarted, so every replica returns cold. Liveness should test only the process; readiness is the right place to admit a dependency is down.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
question: Shown list v4 is [J4, J12, J5]. The user says *hide the Hooli one*, and the assistant shows [J4, J12]. The user then says *open the second one*. Which job should open?
options: J5, because it was second in the original search
J12, because it is second in the list currently on screen
J12, because the tracker remembers it from the previous turn
Ask a clarifying question every time
explain: Ordinals refer to the most recent list the user saw, here shown v6 = [J4, J12]. J12 happens to be second in both lists, but the reason it is right is the current list; the third option names the right job for the wrong reason, and would fail if the lists differed.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Do reasoning models admit the hints they use?
question: A model has n = 4 options. On hinted prompts it switches to the hint at rate p = 0.40 and to another non-hint option at rate q = 0.08. Among hint-switching CoTs, 18% mention the hint. What is the normalized faithfulness score?
explain: alpha = 1 - q/((n-2)p) = 1 - 0.08/(2 x 0.40) = 0.90. Normalized = 0.18/0.90 = 0.20. Normalizing raises the score slightly, because some switches are attributed to noise rather than hint use.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Pinned host memory: the precondition for overlap
question: On which system does switching from pageable to pinned host memory help least, and why?
options: The laptop, because its link is slower so the copy dominates either way
Neither; the ratio is a property of the PCIe generation, not the host
The desktop, because a faster GPU hides the staging copy behind the kernel
The desktop, because its CPU runs the driver's staging memcpy fast enough that staging was not the bottleneck
explain: Pageable transfers were 5.369 GB/s on the desktop against 2.308 GB/s on the laptop, so the desktop's staging memcpy was already near link speed and pinning only added 1.15x there, against 2.50x on the laptop. The bottleneck being removed is host-side, which is why the benefit is a property of the host.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: CUDA Graphs: paying the launch cost once
question: You are capturing on a stream from cudaStreamCreate. During capture you call cudaMemcpy (no stream) to upload a small constant. What happens?
options: The copy is recorded as a memcpy node in the graph
The copy executes immediately and is simply left out of the graph
The capture graph is invalidated, and cudaStreamEndCapture returns an error and a NULL graph
Capture succeeds but the graph can only be launched on the legacy stream
explain: cudaMemcpy enqueues to the legacy stream and synchronizes on it. While a non-blocking-flagless stream is being captured, any use of the legacy stream is invalid, and synchronous APIs are therefore invalid too. An invalid operation during capture invalidates the capture graph, and cudaStreamEndCapture returns an error and a NULL graph.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
question: Why can a search engine cache document embeddings for a bi-encoder but not intermediate document states for a cross-encoder?
options: Cross-encoder hidden states are too large to store
In a cross-encoder every document token attends to the query tokens in every layer, so its states differ for each query
Cross-encoders use random dropout at inference time
Bi-encoders use a different tokenizer that is deterministic
explain: Attention mixes query tokens into each document token's representation from the first layer on. A cache keyed by document would be wrong for every new query. Size is a secondary issue; dropout is off at inference.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
question: A kernel uses 128x128 CTA tiles in FP16 and is still memory bound. Which change raises the tile's arithmetic intensity against global memory?
options: Growing the tile to 256x128
Doubling bK from 32 to 64 while keeping 128x128
Launching more threads per CTA with the same tile
Switching the inputs from FP16 to FP32
explain: Intensity is 2 bM bN / ((bM + bN) s). bK cancels out, thread count does not appear, and FP32 doubles s, halving intensity. 256x128 raises it from 64 to about 85 FLOP per byte, as long as shared memory and registers can hold it.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
question: A 128x256x64 FP16 tile on SM90 with no epilogue carveout. Using the builder's formula, how many stages fit?
explain: One stage is (128 + 256) x 64 x 2 = 49152 bytes, plus 16 bytes of barriers: 49168. 232448 / 49168 = 4.7, so 4 stages. The wider tile buys reuse at the price of pipeline depth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
question: Using Pond's model (local 85 ns, 8-socket pool 155 ns), what is the average miss latency if 25% of misses go to the pool?
options: 120 ns
155 ns
explain: 85 + 0.25 x (155 - 85) = 85 + 17.5 = 102.5 ns. 120 ns would be f = 0.5; 155 ns is all misses on CXL.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Why the pretraining mixture is a decision you cannot skip
question: Why is tuning the mixture directly on downstream benchmarks risky, beyond its cost?
options: Benchmarks are measured in accuracy, not loss
Downstream tuning always picks uniform weights
The mixture can overfit to the specific benchmarks used, which may not reflect the many tasks the model will face
explain: A pretrained model is used for many tasks nobody listed in advance. A mixture tuned to a handful of benchmarks can trade away performance elsewhere. DoReMi deliberately uses no downstream data.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
question: Your GitHub domain is full of auto-generated config files. Which tool addresses this directly?
options: DoReMi, by lowering GitHub's domain weight
A document-level quality filter that drops low-value files inside the domain
Raising the smoothing parameter c
Iterated DoReMi with more rounds
explain: DoReMi can only scale the whole GitHub domain up or down, which also cuts the good code. Removing specific bad documents is a curation job, like phi-1's educational-value classifier.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
question: A teammate measures one cold lookup and finds SoA only 16% faster, so they conclude the split is pointless. What is the strongest reply?
options: The measurement must be wrong; SoA is always 4x faster here
Per-lookup misses are similar, but the searched data is 4x smaller, so across many lookups it stays cached and the gap widens
SoA only helps with SIMD, and binary search is not vectorized
They should switch to a linked list of keyframes
explain: A single cold lookup misses in both layouts on its first few probes. The benefit of a 512-byte index over a 2 KiB one shows up when many lookups reuse the same lines, which is how an animation system runs.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Batch-dependent numerics and the token that flips
question: You must guarantee that one request gets the same tokens no matter what else is in the batch. Which property is the one you actually need?
options: Batch invariance: each output element's reduction order is fixed regardless of batch size and of the request's position in the batch.
Run-to-run determinism of every kernel.
A fixed random seed attached to each request.
Greedy decoding instead of sampling.
explain: Run-to-run determinism is already true of a typical forward pass and does not help, because the batch changes between runs. A seed fixes the sampler, not the logits. Greedy removes the RNG but makes the near-tie worse. Only batch invariance pins the arithmetic your request sees.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
question: A replica computes its election deadline as `time.time() + random_timeout()`, using Python's real clock, while everything else goes through the simulator. What breaks?
options: Nothing: the timeout value still comes from the seeded generator
Replay: the deadline now depends on wall-clock time, so the same seed can schedule different events
Only performance: real clock reads are slower than simulated ones
Safety of the protocol in production
explain: Wall-clock time differs between runs and is unrelated to simulated time, so the deadline, and every event that depends on it, changes from run to run. One leak like this destroys reproducibility for the whole simulation. All time must come from the simulated clock.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
question: Why is autoregressive decoding slow on a GPU even though the GPU can do far more arithmetic per second than one token needs?
options: Each step must wait for the previous token, and each step does little compute per byte of weights read, so the GPU idles on memory traffic
Softmax over the vocabulary is the dominant cost and cannot be parallelized
The KV cache makes every step recompute attention over all earlier tokens from scratch
Causal attention needs more FLOPs than bidirectional attention
explain: Decode is sequential (token t+1 needs token t) and memory-bound: each pass streams all weights to process one token per sequence. A KV cache avoids recomputation; it does not create it. Causal attention actually computes fewer scores than bidirectional attention.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
question: Why can a diffusion LM not use an exact KV cache the way a GPT does?
options: Its vocabulary is too large
It uses grouped-query attention
Bidirectional attention makes every position's keys and values depend on all other positions, which change whenever a mask is filled
Diffusion models have no keys or values
explain: In a causal model, later tokens never affect earlier keys and values, so caching is exact. Without the causal mask, filling any position changes every layer's activations everywhere. Fast-dLLM reuses them approximately because adjacent steps change them very little.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
question: Using the formula, how long does an ideal transfer of a 4096-token Qwen3-32B prompt (256 KiB per token) take over a 400 Gb/s link?
options: About 2.7 ms
About 172 ms
About 344 ms
About 21.5 ms
explain: 4096 x 262,144 B = 1,073,741,824 B (1 GiB). 400 Gb/s is 50 GB/s, so 1.074 GB / 50 GB/s = 21.5 ms. Half of the 43 ms needed for 8192 tokens, because KV size grows linearly with prompt length.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
question: Why does DiskANN's re-ranking with full-precision vectors cost no extra SSD reads?
options: Full vectors are cached in RAM
Each node's full vector is stored in the same disk block as its neighbor list, so it arrives with the read the search already made
Re-ranking uses PQ codes only
It reads all candidates in one big sequential read
explain: The record layout puts the vector next to the adjacency list, inside one 4 KB read. Re-ranking piggybacks on reads the beam search needed anyway. The paper contrasts this with an earlier system that fetched about a hundred candidate vectors at the end, in one burst of random reads.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
question: In the toy example, what happens to the optimal policy as $\beta$ grows very large?
options: It approaches the reference distribution: 50%, 30%, 20%
It puts all mass on B, the highest reward
It becomes uniform over A, B and C
It puts all mass on A, the reference's favorite
explain: Reweighting by $\exp(r/\beta)$ approaches multiplying everything by 1 as $\beta$ grows, so the optimum returns to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. At $\beta = 10$ it is already 49.38%, 32.75%, 17.87%. Small $\beta$ is what collapses it onto B.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Failure modes, fixes, and DPO in production recipes
question: During DPO training your margin and reward accuracy climb steadily, but `rewards/chosen` keeps getting more negative and outputs drift toward degenerate repetitions. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Lower beta so the model can move further from the reference
Add a term that keeps the chosen log-prob up, such as DPOP's penalty or an NLL loss on chosen answers
Train more epochs so the margin saturates
Remove the reference model to save memory
explain: The pattern is likelihood displacement: the gap widens because both answers fall. DPOP's hinge penalty and Llama 3's NLL term (coefficient 0.2) both directly penalize a falling chosen log-prob. Lowering beta or training longer lets drift continue.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
question: An experiment compared 20,000 reads with zero mismatches. The new path actually returns wrong data on 1 read in 100,000. How likely was this clean result?
options: About 1.8 percent
About 18 percent
About 50 percent
About 82 percent
explain: The probability of no mismatch is (1 - 0.00001) to the power 20,000, which is about 0.819. A clean run that short says little about rare bugs; you need roughly 300,000 comparisons for 95 percent confidence at this rate.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: The verifier: proving every path safe before it runs
question: A program loops `for i in 0..N` where N is read from a map value with no upper bound check. The verifier rejects it. Why?
options: Maps cannot be read inside loops
Loops are never allowed in eBPF
The verifier cannot prove the loop terminates within its limits, because N could be any 64-bit value
The JIT does not support loop instructions
explain: Bounded loops are allowed (since v5.3) only if the verifier can show the exit condition is reached within its 1M processed-instruction budget. An unbounded N defeats that proof. Clamping N to a small constant first fixes it.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
question: A model has 250,000 int8 weights (244 KB) and its largest operator reads a 40 KB tensor and writes a 40 KB tensor. The target has 256 KB of flash and 64 KB of SRAM. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, both fit
The weights do not fit in flash
The peak activations (80 KB) do not fit in SRAM
The model must be fp32 to run on a CPU
explain: Weights live in flash: 244 KB is under 256 KB, though tight once code is added. Activations need the peak of input plus output, 80 KB, which is more than 64 KB of SRAM. You would shrink the largest feature map (fewer channels or lower resolution), not the weights.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
question: You replace every 3x3 conv in a model with depthwise separable blocks and the MAC count drops 8x, but measured latency on your phone CPU drops only 2x. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: The MAC formula is wrong
Depthwise layers do few MACs per byte moved, so they are limited by memory traffic and kernel efficiency rather than arithmetic
Separable convolutions use more parameters
Latency always scales exactly with MACs, so the measurement must be wrong
explain: MAC counts ignore memory traffic and kernel quality. A depthwise layer does only k x k MACs per input value, so it is often bound by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic. This is why the pipeline ends with measurement on the device.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: A team trains with a hard rule 'reward = -1 if truncated at 8K tokens' and sees training become unstable as responses approach 8K. Which change follows the DAPO findings?
options: Raise the penalty to -10 so the model learns faster
Remove the correctness reward for long responses
Mask truncated samples from the loss, or ramp the penalty linearly over a soft zone before the limit
Lower the learning rate only for long responses
explain: Overlong filtering (masking) and soft overlong punishment both reduce reward noise from punishing reasoning that was merely cut off. A bigger cliff adds more noise, not less.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs
question: Why does the one-change-per-step constraint in AFAMAP make sense for energy data?
options: Appliances are physically prevented from switching together
It forces the kettle to be modelled separately
It removes the need for training data
It restates the switch continuity principle: at short sample intervals, simultaneous switching is rare, and the constraint shrinks the search enormously
explain: Simultaneous switches are possible (our minute 45), but rare at short sampling intervals. Assuming at most one change per step turns an exponential joint search into one over N single-chain changes, which is what makes the convex relaxation efficient. It is a modelling assumption, so it will occasionally be wrong.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
question: Profiles are cleaned with NFKC, casefold and suffix stripping before indexing. The query parser lowercases the recruiter's text but does nothing else. A recruiter searches `Brightline Labs, Inc.`. What happens?
options: It matches, because lowercasing is enough
It misses: the query key is `brightline labs, inc.` while the indexed key is `brightline labs`
It matches only r3, which was typed the same way
explain: The index stores cleaned keys, so a raw query string with a comma and suffix never equals them. The fix is to run the exact same normalizer on the query side.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: A server handles 20,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections with one thread per connection. Which cost grows directly with the number of *idle* connections?
options: CPU time spent parsing requests
A sleeping thread, with its own stack and kernel task, for every connection
Network bandwidth used by the replies
The number of bytes each request contains
explain: Parsing and bandwidth scale with *active* traffic. An idle connection does no work, but in thread-per-connection it still owns a whole thread: a stack, a kernel task, and a place in the scheduler. An event loop keeps only a small per-connection record instead.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: A Node service handles 4 slow password hashes (crypto.pbkdf2, about 100 ms each) at the same moment that 4 requests call fs.readFile. With the default pool, what do the file reads experience?
options: They queue behind the hashes on the 4-thread pool, so they finish roughly 100 ms later than they otherwise would
Nothing, file reads use epoll and never touch the pool
They run on the loop thread and block it
Node starts 4 extra threads automatically for file I/O
explain: Both async pbkdf2 and fs calls run on libuv's shared thread pool, which has 4 threads by default. The hashes occupy all 4, so the file reads wait about one hash duration. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE or moving hashing elsewhere fixes it. Disk files cannot use epoll at all.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals by bootstrapping over queries
question: Two systems' per-query nDCG@10 values correlate at 0.9 across 100 queries. Compared with an unpaired bootstrap, what does a paired bootstrap of the mean difference give?
options: A wider interval, because pairing loses degrees of freedom
The same interval, because the means are identical either way
A much narrower interval, because shared query difficulty cancels in the per-query differences
An interval centered on a different value
explain: The point estimate is the same mean difference either way. With strong correlation, most per-query variation is query difficulty that hits both systems alike. Differencing per query removes it, so the variance of the difference is much smaller than the sum of the two variances.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
question: Under the model with h = 1, C = 100 and b = 50, what is the slowdown S for 8 threads sharing one line?
explain: S = k(1 + C/(b h)) = 8 x (1 + 100/50) = 8 x 3 = 24. The 808 answer is the b = 1 worst case, and 3 forgets to multiply by k: all k threads' writes go through one line, one at a time.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
question: Client A (54 examples) returns 0.10, client B (36) returns 0.80, client C (18) returns 2.70, but this round client B drops out and never reports. What does FedAvg set as the new global model?
options: 0.767, since the weights 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108 are properties of the clients
0.500, the weighted average with client B's contribution set to zero
0.750, the weighted average of A and C renormalized over 72 examples
The round is discarded, because FedAvg requires every selected client
explain: The denominator is m_t, the examples in this round only: 54 + 18 = 72. So the model is (54/72) x 0.10 + (18/72) x 2.70 = 0.075 + 0.675 = 0.750. Keeping stale weights that sum to less than one (option B) would shrink the model toward zero, and single dropouts never abandon a round.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower
question: Your DP federated run has far worse accuracy than the non-private baseline at the same epsilon. Which change most directly fixes it, according to the published results?
options: Sample many more users per round, so the same noise is averaged over more clipped updates
Lower the clipping norm S, so each update contributes less
Reduce the number of rounds, since every round spends privacy budget
Switch from user-level to example-level accounting and report that instead
explain: Noise is added once per round to the average, so more users per round shrinks its relative size at fixed epsilon: matching the baseline needed about 5000 users per round instead of 100, roughly 60x the compute. Lowering S adds clipping bias, and with large populations extra rounds cost very little budget (epsilon moved from 0.84 to 0.88 over a million rounds at 1e9 users).

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
question: An MoE layer has 16 experts, each the same size as the dense MLP it replaced, with top-2 routing. Compared with the dense MLP, what happens to parameters and per-token FLOPs in that layer?
options: Both grow 16 times
Parameters grow 2 times; FLOPs grow 16 times
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs grow about 2 times, plus a tiny router cost
Parameters grow 16 times; per-token FLOPs stay exactly the same as dense
explain: Every expert is stored, so parameters scale with N = 16. Each token runs only K = 2 experts, so expert FLOPs are 2 times the dense MLP. The router (one dot product per expert) adds a little on top. With top-1 routing (Switch), expert FLOPs would match the dense MLP.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
question: A team copies V3's recipe but trains with very small global batches (a few sequences per step). Which risk grows most?
options: Future-token leakage from the bias
The shared expert stops training
Node-limited routing stops working
Per-step load imbalance, since batch-wise balancing cannot even out a batch that is mostly one domain, so busy experts stall the step
explain: The loss-free paper shows balance improving as the computation batch grows, and the V3 report lists imbalance within small batches as a challenge that large-scale expert and data parallelism solves. The bias uses only past batches, so there is no leakage.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 forward: when the exponential is the bottleneck
question: Why does FlashAttention-4 emulate only 10 to 25% of exponentials in software instead of all of them?
options: The polynomial is too inaccurate for more than a quarter of the row
Emulation uses extra registers, register bandwidth and latency; doing all of them would cause spills and leave MUFU idle
FMA units can only process one row in four
MUFU is faster than the FMA units for every input
explain: The goal is to split the work between two units that can run in parallel. The paper says full emulation would raise register pressure and could cause spills that cancel the gain, so the fraction is tuned to the MMA-to-exp ratio of each tile shape. Accuracy is not the limit: after BF16 rounding the polynomial matches hardware.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Attention states, cascade attention and composable formats
question: Partial states for one query: prefix $(O = 2.0, \mathrm{LSE} = 0)$ and suffix $(O = 6.0, \mathrm{LSE} = 0)$. What is the merged output?
options: 6.0, the larger LSE wins
It cannot be computed without the raw scores
explain: Equal LSEs mean both halves carry equal total softmax mass, so the weights are $e^0/(e^0+e^0) = 0.5$ each and $O = 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0.5 \cdot 6 = 4.0$. The merged LSE is $\log 2$. The states alone are enough; that is the whole point of the operator.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
question: Which statement about conditional flow matching is correct?
options: It needs the marginal velocity field computed over the whole dataset at every step
It only works with straight-line paths
Regressing onto per-sample conditional velocities gives the same gradient as regressing onto the intractable marginal velocity
It trains by maximizing the log-likelihood of the data under the ODE
explain: Lipman et al. Theorem 2: the CFM and FM losses differ by a constant independent of the parameters, so their gradients match. Straight OT paths are one choice; diffusion-style Gaussian paths also fit the framework.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
question: A race fires in 1 of every 184,756 equally likely orders. Your CI runs the test 1,000 times a day, each run picking an order at random. Which statement is closest to right?
options: Over a week you have roughly a 4% chance of having seen the bug even once
After a week of green runs the code is very likely correct
The bug is impossible in practice because its probability is so small
Running the test on more cores makes the bug certain to appear
explain: 7,000 runs give $1-(1-1/184756)^{7000} \approx 3.7\%$. Green CI says little here. Rare orders still happen in production, where the same code runs billions of times; AWS noted that improbability is not a defense against such bugs.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
question: Which statement about Verus ghost code is true?
options: Spec functions can use u32 overflow semantics to match the code
Proof functions run at startup to check the lemmas
Spec and proof code are erased before compilation, so they add no run-time cost
Exec code may call spec functions to compute values at run time
explain: Ghost code exists only for verification. Spec functions use mathematical int and nat, proof functions are checked statically, and exec code cannot call either to compute run-time values.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
question: Why does NVFP4 need a per-tensor FP32 scale while MXFP4 does not?
options: FP32 scales make the GEMM run faster
E4M3 block scales cover a much narrower range than E8M0 (at most 448 and at least 2^-9), so the tensor must first be shifted so all its block scales fit
Because NVFP4 elements are E4M3 instead of E2M1
To store the sign of each block
explain: E8M0 spans 2^-127 to 2^127, enough for any block scale. E4M3 trades that range for 3 mantissa bits. The FP32 tensor scale maps the largest block scale onto 448 so the rest fit underneath.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: The write-ahead rule: flush the log first, pages later
question: During redo, a record for page P has LSN 500. The page as read from disk has page LSN 730. What does recovery do?
options: Apply the record, since redo replays every record after the checkpoint
Stop recovery: the page is newer than the log, so it is corrupt
Skip the record: the page already contains this change and later ones
Roll the page back to LSN 500
explain: The page was written after records up to 730 were applied, so the change at 500 is already in it. Applying only when the record LSN exceeds the page LSN is what makes redo safe to repeat.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
question: A teammate initializes the first row as `prev = [0] * (len(b) + 1)` instead of `list(range(len(b) + 1))`. What does the function now compute?
options: The same Levenshtein distance, because row 0 is overwritten anyway
The cost of matching `a` against the best substring of `b` that ends at its last character, because skipping a prefix of `b` becomes free
Always 0
The longest common subsequence length
explain: Row 0 says how much it costs to consume a prefix of `b` before `a` starts. Setting it to 0 makes that free, so a match may start anywhere in `b`. Sellers used exactly this change in 1980 to turn the distance algorithm into approximate substring search. It is a useful algorithm, but not Levenshtein distance.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
question: A Levenshtein automaton for query `fuzzy` with k = 1 reaches a state where every entry of the DP row is 2 after reading `ja`. Why can it reject every term starting with `ja` without reading further?
options: Because terms starting with ja are rare
Because the row minimum never decreases as more characters are read, so the final distance will be at least 2
Because the automaton only accepts terms of exactly 5 characters
Because Lucene sets prefix_length to 2
explain: Each new cell is at least the minimum of the previous row (diagonal moves add 0 or 1, the others add 1), so a row whose minimum is 2 can only lead to distances of 2 or more. That dead state lets the engine skip the entire ja block of the sorted term dictionary.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Searching code space: kd-trees, tolerance and why quads beat triangles
question: You double the code-match tolerance to cope with a noisy camera. In the uniform toy model, by what factor do chance matches per query grow for quads?
options: 2x
4x
8x
explain: The query region is a 4D ball whose volume grows as t to the 4th power, so doubling t multiplies chance matches by 16. For 2D triangle codes it would be 4x. This is why quads tolerate a larger index before verification costs explode.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
question: A ship-tracking query in Fiji uses `WHERE lon >= 179.5 AND lon <= -179.5` to find ships within about 50 km of the antimeridian. It returns zero rows even though ships are there. What is the fix?
options: Swap the bounds to lon >= -179.5 AND lon <= 179.5
Convert longitudes to radians before comparing
Split the box into two: lon >= 179.5 OR lon <= -179.5
Use a larger box so the bounds no longer cross 180
explain: The interval wraps around 180, so no single number is both at least 179.5 and at most -179.5. The correct region is the union of two ranges. Swapping the bounds selects almost the whole planet instead, and a larger box still wraps.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Tree indexes: R-trees, PostGIS GiST and Lucene BKD
question: A PostGIS query uses `geom && query_box` to count census blocks in a neighborhood and gets a much larger number than expected. Why?
options: The GiST index is stale and needs VACUUM ANALYZE
&& compares bounding boxes only, so blocks whose boxes touch the neighborhood's box are counted even if the shapes do not intersect
&& uses meters while the data is in degrees
&& rounds coordinates to 4-byte integers
explain: && is the index-only bounding box test. It is the fast first pass; an exact predicate like ST_Intersects must refine the result. Statistics affect the plan's speed, not which rows match.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Color conversion: a 3x3 matrix per pixel, with the right coefficients
question: A grayscale conversion of HD footage uses the 0.299, 0.587, 0.114 row. What is the effect?
options: Any non-neutral pixel's luma is biased, by 13 levels for a mid green-ish pixel and up to about 32 levels for saturated green
No effect, since luma rows differ only by a scale factor
Only saturated reds change, because red's coefficient differs the most
The image becomes brighter overall by a constant offset that can be subtracted out
explain: The rows are not proportional: green goes from 0.587 to 0.7152 and blue from 0.114 to 0.0722. The error depends on the pixel's hue, so it is neither a constant offset nor confined to one channel. For our four sample pixels the gap ranges from 1 to 32 levels, with green worst because its weight moved most.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
question: In the final state, memory_allocated() reports 27 MiB but tensors requested only 25 MiB. Where did the 2 extra MiB go?
options: Two unsplit leftovers of 1 MiB each, attached to D and F
Event bookkeeping for streams
The rounding of 7 MiB up to 8 MiB
Metadata headers stored in device memory
explain: D asked for 4 MiB and got a 5 MiB block; F asked for 14 MiB and got 15 MiB. In both cases the remainder (1 MiB) was not more than 1 MiB, so the large pool refused to split. allocated_bytes counts whole blocks; requested_bytes counts what tensors asked for.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
question: Which level of the hierarchy is shared by every SM on the GPU?
options: Shared memory
The L2 cache
The register file
The L1 cache
explain: Shared memory, L1 and registers are per SM. The Programming Guide describes L2 as located on the device and shared among all the SMs, which is why one kernel's wasteful traffic can slow every other SM.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
question: A teammate drops `__syncthreads()` from the tiled transpose because "each thread only touches its own data." What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the barrier only affects performance
Threads read tile elements written by other warps, so they may read before those writes happen
Without the barrier the global writes become uncoalesced
The barrier is needed only when the tile is padded
explain: Thread (x, y) stores tile[y+j][x] but later reads tile[x][y+j], an element another thread, often in another warp, stored. The NVIDIA transpose post requires `__syncthreads()` because threads write different data to odata than they read from idata, and the CUDA guide says synchronization is necessary when threads of a block share shared memory addresses.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
question: You profile with `--set full` and the application takes 30 times longer, but the reported kernel durations are unchanged. What is the right reading?
options: The durations are stale and should be taken from Nsight Systems instead
The kernels have become slower and the tool is hiding it
Expected: a full metric set needs many replay passes plus save, restore and flush around each, none of which is included in the reported duration
Software-patched metrics have inflated the reported duration
explain: More metrics means more passes, and the per-pass preparation and post-processing is explicitly not included in the reported duration. The documentation notes the same thing in reverse: because of that overhead you cannot derive a kernel's duration from host timers or CUDA events while profiling with Nsight Compute. Duration is also never collected in a software-patching pass, so those metrics do not distort it.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters
question: A kernel uses a 48 KB shared-memory tile and `__syncthreads()`. A teammate proposes having block 7 read the tile that block 3 just loaded, to save a global memory read. When is that allowed?
options: Always: shared memory is shared by the whole grid
Never, under any launch configuration
Only if blocks 3 and 7 are in the same thread block cluster, using distributed shared memory and cluster.sync() on compute capability 9.0 or later
Only if both blocks call __syncthreads() first
explain: Ordinary shared memory is private to one block. Clusters (CC 9.0+) let blocks in the same cluster map each other's shared memory, because the cluster's blocks are co-scheduled. With a portable cluster size of at most 8, blocks 3 and 7 would need a cluster shape that contains both, which a 1D cluster of 8 starting at block 0 does. __syncthreads() never reaches across blocks.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
question: After merging, the node QUILLFERN LABS has descriptions from 3 chunks and BEN ORTIZ has one. How many description-summarization LLM calls do these two nodes need?
explain: Only lists with more than one description are sent to the LLM. QUILLFERN LABS needs 1 call; BEN ORTIZ keeps its single description as is.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
question: In HippoRAG's PPR step, why does Quillfern Labs score high for the question about Ben Ortiz and Rover X2, even though the question never mentions it?
options: Because random walks restarting at both seeds pass through it, so it collects probability from both sides
Because it has the longest description
Because the LLM ranked it first
Because it is in the largest community
explain: PPR mass flows outward from the seed nodes. A node adjacent to both seeds receives probability from each, which is how the bridge in a multi-hop chain surfaces without an extra retrieval round.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: The GRPO objective token by token: clipping, averaging and KL
question: In DeepSeekMath's setup the policy takes exactly one gradient step per batch of sampled outputs. What does the clip term do in that step?
options: It clips every token whose advantage is negative
It halves the learning rate for long outputs
It replaces the KL penalty
Nothing: the ratio is exactly 1, so the clipped and unclipped terms are equal
explain: With one update per batch, pi_theta equals pi_old when the loss is evaluated, so every ratio is 1, well inside [1 - eps, 1 + eps]. The objective reduces to a policy gradient weighted by the group advantages, plus the KL term.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Service days, calendar exceptions and times past 24:00
question: A feed has WKDY in calendar.txt (Mon to Fri) and a row WKDY, 20260704, exception_type 1 for Saturday July 4. What happens on July 4?
options: Nothing, Saturdays are 0 in calendar.txt so the exception is ignored
The feed is invalid because the date is outside the weekly pattern
Only trips with times past 24:00:00 run
All WKDY trips run on July 4 as an added service day
explain: exception_type 1 adds service on that date even though the weekly pattern says no. calendar_dates.txt modifies calendar.txt; that is exactly how special event or holiday services are added.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
question: A hot function has IPC 0.25 and 20 last-level cache misses per 1000 instructions. Which change is most likely to make it faster?
options: Rewrite it to execute 10% fewer instructions with the same memory access pattern
Change the data layout so consecutive iterations touch the same cache lines
Compile with a higher optimization level to shorten the instruction sequence
Run it on a core with a wider decoder
explain: Low IPC with many cache misses means the core is mostly waiting on memory. Removing instructions or widening the front end does little while every miss still stalls. Better locality cuts the misses that the cycles are actually spent on.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Reading the numbers: generic events, pitfalls and top-down
question: TopdownL1 shows 60% backend bound, and drilling down shows most of it is memory bound. IPC is 0.4. Which next step fits best?
options: Reduce branch mispredictions with likely/unlikely hints
Shrink the binary so it fits in the instruction cache
Sample a cache-miss event with :pp to find the loads responsible, then improve their locality
Ignore it: backend bound means the CPU is doing useful work
explain: Memory bound means slots are lost waiting on data. Bad speculation and frontend fixes target other buckets. Precise sampling on a miss event points at the exact loads to restructure.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: With the defaults, what does setting khugepaged/max_ptes_none to 0 trade away?
options: Faults no longer allocate huge pages
khugepaged will not collapse any range with even one unpopulated PTE, so sparse regions stay on 4 KiB pages but never bloat
Huge pages can no longer be swapped
khugepaged stops running
explain: max_ptes_none only governs collapse: at 0, a range must have all 512 PTEs populated. That removes collapse-induced bloat but fewer ranges become huge. Fault-time allocation is controlled by enabled and defrag, not this knob.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers
question: Jamba-v0.1's config has 32 layers, attn_layer_period 8 and attn_layer_offset 4. Which layers (0-based) are attention?
